analysis.one_liner: Bans candy, fruit, and other flavors in e-cigarettes, cigars, and smokeless tobacco.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended, despite 24 cosponsors including two Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to sell flavored non-cigarette tobacco products, including e-cigarettes, vape pens, and flavored cigars. It was aimed at the surge in youth vaping, which the bill's own findings say rose 78 percent among high school students in a single year. An e-cigarette flavor could stay on the market only if the FDA found the maker had shown it helps smokers quit without hooking kids. The bill sat in committee and never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would be far less likely to start using nicotine, since the bill's findings note that 81 percent of youth who ever used tobacco started with a flavored product and that flavors are a main reason kids vape. Parents and schools also gain from reduced youth addiction and the poison-control calls tied to candy-style e-liquid packaging.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and teens at risk of nicotine addiction

how_it_helps.text: Bans characterizing flavors — strawberry, grape, cotton candy, gummy bear and roughly 15,000 others the bill cites — from all non-cigarette tobacco products, including e-cigarettes and cigars, one year after enactment.

Targets the youth vaping epidemic the bill documents: in 2018 youth e-cigarette use rose 78 percent among high schoolers and 48 percent among middle schoolers, with more than 3.6 million youth users and 82 percent of current youth vapers saying they vape 'because they come in flavors I like.'

Keeps a narrow door open for harm reduction: an e-cigarette flavor could remain legal only if the FDA found the manufacturer proved it increases smoking cessation among adults, does not increase youth initiation, and does not increase user harm.

analysis.who_pays: E-cigarette and vape companies, which lose their flavor-driven product lines, and flavored cigar makers, for whom flavored products made up more than half of the convenience store cigar market. Adult vapers who used flavored products to quit cigarettes bear a cost too, since their flavors would be off the shelf unless the FDA approved them one by one. The FDA bears the burden of running the case-by-case approval process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Vape companies and flavored cigar makers

drawbacks.text: Adults who quit cigarettes by vaping flavored products would lose access to those flavors unless the manufacturer won a separate FDA order proving each flavor helps cessation, does not hook kids, and does not harm users — a high bar that could push some adults back to smoking.

The bill exempts cigarettes entirely, so menthol cigarettes — the flavor that dominates the cigarette market and is heavily used by young smokers — would stay on store shelves while flavored alternatives to cigarettes are banned.

The FDA-approval pathway requires a case-by-case determination for every flavor and every manufacturer, an administrative burden that could mean years of delay even for flavors with solid evidence behind them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: kids lose the flavored products that get them addicted, and some adults who quit smoking with flavored vapes lose a tool that worked for them unless the FDA signs off flavor by flavor. The cigarette exemption is the biggest design flaw — Congress would ban flavored competitors to cigarettes while leaving menthol cigarettes untouched. On balance, the public-health gain for the millions of minors documented in the bill's findings outweighs the industry cost, but the bill was not crafted to protect adult quitters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dick Durbin introduced the bill on March 5, 2019, together with Senator Lisa Murkowski, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee that same day.

The bill would have banned characterizing flavors in all non-cigarette tobacco products, including e-cigarettes and cigars, effective one year after enactment, with a limited FDA process to authorize e-cigarette flavors proven to help adults quit without increasing youth use.
It drew 24 cosponsors — 22 Democrats and 2 Republicans — but received no committee action of any kind after the referral.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died in committee without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: E-cigarette and flavored cigar makers, who kept selling the flavored products the bill would have banned, and adult vapers who kept their flavors without any new FDA process.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it as chief sponsor.

for.name: Lisa Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

for.name: 24 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, building a bipartisan list of supporters.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote in the two years it sat in his committee.

against.name: E-cigarette and vaping industry
against.role: Manufacturers, retailers, and vape trade groups
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against flavor bans and pushed Congress to leave flavored vape products on the market.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor joined by a Republican co-introducer and 22 other Democrats plus 2 Republicans — and the bill died without any recorded vote that would show opposition.

industries.note: The bill eliminates the flavored products — the industry cited more than 15,000 unique flavors — that drove the surge in youth use and the bulk of industry growth, allowing only FDA-approved flavors proven to aid adult cessation. Its business model depended on flavors the bill's findings tie directly to teen uptake.

Flavored cigars made up more than half the convenience store cigar market in 2015 and were sold for as little as 3 for 99 cents; the bill bans those flavors outright. The bill's findings link flavored cigars to youth cigar smoking, particularly among high school boys.

The bill exempts cigarettes, so menthol cigarettes stay fully legal while flavored alternatives to cigarettes face a ban. That hands cigarette makers a protected market over competing products whose flavors draw users away from cigarettes.
